name: Dana Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Dana, thank you for doing this. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm 27 and I'm a marketing specialist at Hillside Roasters, a coffee brand that sells beans in supermarkets and by subscription online. My day is mostly online ads and subscription emails: I set the budgets, write the ads, and check every morning which ones brought in new subscribers. I use AI tools all day, for drafts, for the ad images, for sorting through the customer reviews.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the speed. I can test an idea at nine and know by lunch whether people bite. What wears me down is the money: the pay's on the low side, Tomas, my partner, is an electrician who's just gone self-employed, and between us we've got about three weeks of savings. Marketing jobs are thin on the ground here; the next nearest brand is two towns away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into using AI so much?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I just tried everything as it came out. My manager, Anya, lets me run with it as long as the numbers are good. I'm the one who set up the tools for the rest of the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it stays a fancy helper. That's fine by me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are handy and the hype was overdone. I'd share a post with the five tricks that actually saved me time. I'm not going to pretend I was right all along, though, because I thought it would be bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's okay in that world, but our money isn't great. Tomas's work comes in lumps, some months loads and some months almost nothing, and we've got barely anything saved. Hillside also lost one supermarket deal this year, which made everyone a bit jumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the tools as I do now. I'd set up a little side thing doing ads for local cafés, maybe three of them at a hundred a month each. And I'd make us a rule: whenever Tomas has a good month, a third goes straight into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. A bit itchy for more, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cafés would you approach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's the one by the station that does great cakes and has an empty social media page. And a new one on the High Street run by two sisters who keep asking how to get more people in. I'd show them a month of results before asking for money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the lost supermarket deal affect things at Hillside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They froze hiring and cut the summer party. My manager said our jobs were safe, but she said it in the voice people use when they're not sure. I made sure my numbers were the best they'd ever been that month.

say: I'd say the tools are **handy** and the hype was overdone.
I'd share the **five tricks** that actually saved me time.
think: I think my **job's okay**, but our money isn't great.
Tomas's **self-employed work** comes in lumps, and Hillside lost a supermarket deal.
do: Keep using the **AI tools** for drafts and ad images.
Run ads for **three local cafés** at a hundred a month each.
Save **a third** of every good month Tomas has.
feel: I feel **pretty steady**, a bit **itchy** for more.
S0.quote: My manager said our jobs were safe, but she said it in the voice people use when they're not sure.
fieldNote: Her worry is **lumpy household income**, not AI.
She looks for **side income** even when things are calm.
She read her manager's **tone** and responded by working harder.

steps.text: Keep running Hillside's ads with AI drafts and images
Offer the station café a free first month of ads
Save a third of each good month Tomas has

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's pretty much what I think is happening already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the tools, because the people who use them will replace the people who don't. I'd also say firms should help their staff learn, not just cut. I'd be the one at work running sessions on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in the better spot, because I'm already the AI person at Hillside. I'd probably end up doing what three people do now, with software. The risk is that once it's all set up, they don't need me to run it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Anya with a plan to automate the whole ad and email side, and ask to be paid more for running it. I'd grow the café work to five or six clients, so there's a second income. I'd also apply for remote jobs with bigger brands in the city, since I can do this from anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. I like a puzzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they might not need you to run it either. When would you start worrying about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The day they stop asking me for new ideas and only ask me to check the outputs, I'm a button-presser, and button-pressers get cut. I'd want to be out or promoted before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben, who writes our product descriptions. He's lovely, but he's slow with new things. I'd make him sit with me for an hour a week, whether he wants to or not.

I'd say firms should **help staff learn**, not just cut.
think: I think I'm in a **better spot** as the AI person.
Once it's set up, they might not **need me** to run it.
do: Pitch Anya a plan to **automate** ads and email, for more pay.
Grow café work to **five or six clients**.
Apply for **remote jobs** with bigger brands in the city.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but mostly **excited**, like a puzzle.
S1.quote: The day they stop asking me for new ideas and only ask me to check the outputs, I'm a button-presser, and button-pressers get cut.
fieldNote: She sees herself as a **winner for now**, but spots the trap.
Her test is clear: **new ideas** versus checking outputs.
She'd pull a slow **colleague** along rather than leave him behind.

steps.text: Pitch Anya a plan to automate Hillside's ads and emails
Grow café ad work to five or six clients
Apply for remote marketing jobs with bigger city brands

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That changes everything, doesn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a proper national plan, and fast, because nobody's ready. I'd tell friends to stop thinking about careers and start thinking about the next three years. I'd be blunt, but not hysterical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my job's gone by 2028, and being good with the tools won't save it, because the tools won't need me. The bright side is Tomas: robots for hands-on work don't come until about 2031, and even then wiring old houses is messy. My partner Tomas does electrical work, and in a fast AGI world, his work is our lifeboat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start helping Tomas straight away: his invoices, quotes and bookings, then carrying cable on jobs. I'd ask him about doing an electrical apprenticeship with him, so I'm a second pair of hands by the time my job goes. We'd cut back to basics and hold on to every penny. And I'd claim whatever support the government brings in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Weirdly practical too. My brain goes to lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Tomas feel about you joining him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh first, then say yes. He's always said I'd be better on site than I think. The question is whether there's enough work for two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second phone contract and the car Tomas doesn't use for work. We'd stop eating out completely. Then the holiday to see my sister, which hurts.

say: I'd say we need a **national plan**, fast.
I'd tell friends to think about the **next three years**, not careers.
think: I think my **job's gone** by 2028, tools or no tools.
Tomas's **electrical work** is our lifeboat until robots come around 2031.
do: Do Tomas's **invoices and quotes**, then carry cable on jobs.
Cut to **basics** and claim any new support.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, but **practical**, like my brain goes to lists.
S2.quote: My partner Tomas does electrical work, and in a fast AGI world, his work is our lifeboat.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** and pivots to her partner's trade at once.
She sees **hands-on work** as a bridge, not a forever answer.
Her **lists** are her way of coping with fear.

steps.text: Start an electrical apprenticeship working with Tomas
Cut the second phone contract and sell the spare car
Claim any job-loss support the government brings in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to do something properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so firms should start retraining people now and be honest about which jobs are going. I'd say it at work, kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think marketing's done for me by 2031. But five years is enough to get qualified as an electrician alongside Tomas, and robots don't come for that until about 2034. That's a real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job at Hillside for two or three years, run all the AI and save hard. I'd start a part-time electrical course next year and help Tomas at weekends. I'd also take on his paperwork, so his business grows while I train. By 2030 I'd want to be on site full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in charge. I hate not having a plan, and this one's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in marketing you'd keep, once you're an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas's own marketing, obviously. His website's terrible. I'd make us the electricians everyone in town finds first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family think of you swapping marketing for electrics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say she paid for university for nothing, and my dad would say good, a real trade. I'd say both of them are a bit right.

say: I'd say firms should **retrain people now** and be honest about jobs.
I'd raise it at work **kindly**, not to scare anyone.
think: I think marketing's **done for me** by 2031.
I can **qualify as an electrician** before robots come around 2034.
do: Keep my Hillside job and **save hard** for two or three years.
Start a **part-time electrical course** next year.
feel: I feel **anxious, but in charge**, because this is a plan.
S3.quote: My mum would say she paid for university for nothing, and my dad would say good, a real trade.
fieldNote: The **extra years** let her move from marketing to a trade in steps.
She'd turn her skills to **her partner's business**.
Her **family** splits on the change, and she sees both sides.

steps.text: Start a part-time electrical course next year
Save hard while staying at Hillside for two or three years
Rebuild Tomas's website and take over his quotes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty of runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to prepare properly and there's no excuse not to. I'd post about how people can start planning now without panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could do very well in marketing for five or six years, being the person who runs the AI. Then I'd move into Tomas's business, which by then could be bigger. I'm not scared of this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hillside and push for a promotion as the AI lead. I'd start running Tomas's business side properly: his website, his bookings, his ads. In a few years we'd buy a second van and hire an apprentice, and I'd do my own electrical qualification over time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mostly curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a second van is a big step on three weeks of savings. How would you do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on three weeks, obviously. We'd save for three or four years first. Ten years gives us that, which two years doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything else for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably get married, which we've been putting off because of money. Ten years feels like enough time to plan a life, not just a scramble.

say: I'd say there's **no excuse** not to prepare properly.
I'd post about how people can start **planning now**, calmly, without panicking or quitting anything yet.
think: I think I could do **very well** in marketing for five or six years.
Then I'd move into **Tomas's business**, which could be bigger by then.
do: Push Hillside for a **promotion** as the AI lead.
Save for **a second van** and an apprentice in a few years.
feel: I feel a bit **uneasy**, but mostly **curious**.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like enough time to plan a life, not just a scramble.
fieldNote: With a decade, she sees **opportunity** more than threat.
Her plan rests on **her partner's trade** growing into a family business.
A long warning lets them think about **marriage**.

steps.text: Push for a promotion as Hillside's AI lead

Plan the wedding they've put off for money

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My job goes and we'd be living on Tomas's lumpy income with nothing saved. What would help is cheap, fast training in trades, and some help for small businesses like his to take people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about partners. Half of what I'd do depends on Tomas having a job with his hands. If my partner and I were both in marketing, I'd be telling you a very different story.

headlineQuote: If my partner and I were both in marketing, I'd be telling you a very different story.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old ads specialist** at a coffee brand, using AI tools all day.
Her partner Tomas is a **self-employed electrician**, and they have three weeks saved.
She's pragmatic and centrist, and focused on **what works**, not who's to blame.
She stays **uneasy** in the milder pictures and becomes **alarmed** only at AGI by 2028.
Her backup is to **join Tomas's trade** and grow his business.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when she'd lose her job with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Help for **small businesses** to take people on.
